attempts.raw_response: The world-mountain, with its summit in the heavens and its roots in the underworld, represents one of the most persistent symbols in ancient religious thought. This conception appears in the Babylonian ziggurat, the Hindu Meru, and the Scandinavian Yggdrasil, each embodying the same fundamental idea of a cosmic pillar connecting the three realms of existence. The Phoenicians, with their remarkable talent for synthesizing foreign elements, transmitted this concept along with their other religious traditions to the Mediterranean world. The Greeks transformed it into the Titan Atlas, condemned to uphold the celestial vault for eternity. In the Hindu system, Mount Meru serves as the axis around which the universe revolves, its peak reaching into the highest heavens while its base extends into the lowest depths of the cosmic waters. This parallelism suggests a common origin in the ancient Accadian and Sumerian theological speculation, though each culture developed the motif according to its own peculiar genius and cosmological requirements.

pair.human_continuation:
Under its other name, "Kharsak-kurra," or "Mountain of the East,"
it was identified with the present Mount Elwend, and was regarded as the
spot where the ark had rested, and where the gods had their seat. A
reference is made to it in Isa. xiv. 13. Both hymns illustrate the imagery
and metaphor out of which grew the mythology of primeval Babylonia, and
offer curious parallels to the Aryan hymns of the Rig-Veda. The cuneiform
texts are lithographed in the "Cuneiform Inscriptions of Western Asia,"
Vol. IV, 27, I, 2.



TWO ACCADIAN HYMNS


I


1   O shepherd,[1] Lord Tammuz, Bridegroom[2] of Istar!
2   Lord of Hades, Lord of Tul-Sukhba!
3   _Understanding_ one, who among the papyri the water drinks
    not!
pair.prefix:
143). The myth of Tammuz and
Istar passed, through the Phoenicians, to the Greeks, among whom Adonis
and Aphrodite represent the personages of the ancient Accadian legend.
Tammuz is referred to in Ezek. viii. 14. (See "Records of the Past," Vol.
IX, p. 147.) The second hymn treats of the world-mountain, the Atlas of
the Greeks, which supports the heaven with its stars, and is rooted in
Hades.
